item.title: Financial Incentives and Inequalities in Dental Care Delivery
item.description:
Importance: Patients with no prior relationship with a National Health Service (NHS) general dental practice in primary care are less likely to successfully obtain a dental appointment compared with returning patients. As part of a post-COVID-19 pandemic NHS Dental Recovery Plan, a new patient premium (NPP) scheme was introduced in England from March 1, 2024, to encourage dental practices to treat patients who had not seen an NHS dentist in the past 2 years.

Objective: To assess whether the NPP scheme was associated with an increase in dental care utilization under the NHS.

Design, setting, and participants: This pooled cross-sectional study analyzed a national panel dataset of monthly dental activity data between March 2023 and March 2025 in England, using an interrupted time series approach with segmented regression analysis. All primary care practices that submitted claims for general dental services under the NHS were included.

Exposure: Implementation of the NPP.

Main outcomes and measures: Number of new dental patients, total number of dental patients, and units of dental activity delivered.

Results: A total of 4 377 699 new patients were seen under the NPP scheme; the mean (SD) count of adult patients was 235 380 (41 394) per month preintervention and 205 235 (18 950) postintervention, and of children was 140 502 (19 379) per month preintervention and 131 511 (14 752) per month postintervention. At the aggregate national level in England, there was no significant association between the NPP and the total number of new NHS dental patients. There was a monthly decline in new patients prior to (β, -76; 95% CI, -118 to -34) and at the point of (β, -665; 95% CI, -928 to -402) introduction of the NPP. There was a positive trend change after the NPP was implemented (β, 117; 95% CI, 58 to 175), driven primarily by an increase in the number of new adult patients and patients requiring band 2 and 3 treatments. Post-NPP trends varied across integrated care boards (ICBs). In ICBs where there was an increase in the number of new patients post-NPP, the total number of patients and dental activity delivered remained relatively constant or declined over time.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of all NHS dental practices in England, implementation of the NPP was associated with an increase in the number of underserved new patients, but results varied by geographical area. Findings suggested a potential substitution effect whereby new patients displaced returning patients under the NHS in the absence of a corresponding increase in dental capacity.

item.title: Applying Target Trial Emulation in Vaccine Research: A Scoping Review
item.description:
Importance: Target trial emulation (TTE) has emerged as a rigorous framework for strengthening causal inference in observational research, following the design principles of randomized clinical trials using clinical data. While TTE is increasingly applied in vaccine effectiveness and safety evaluations, its implementation, reporting practices, and alignment with regulatory standards for real-world evidence remain poorly characterized.

Objective: To evaluate the methodological rigor, reporting completeness, and regulatory alignment of observational vaccine studies that emulate a target trial.

Evidence review: PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2021 and August 2025 that used clinical data to assess vaccine effectiveness or safety. Eligible studies explicitly or implicitly emulated a target trial through comparative, causal inference-based designs. Two reviewers independently screened and extracted data on adherence to TTE core design components (ie, eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment procedures, follow-up, outcomes, causal contrasts, and analysis plans) and alignment with regulatory real-world evidence guidance.

Findings: Among 79 studies meeting inclusion criteria, 58 covered COVID-19, 19 covered influenza, and 12 covered other vaccine-preventable diseases, including herpes zoster, mpox, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and other diseases. Only 25 studies (31.6%) reported clearly documented protocols. Although most studies delineated eligibility criteria, exposures, and outcomes, validation of operational definitions was infrequent (eligibility: 4 studies [5.1%]; exposure: 4 studies [5.1%]; outcome: 14 studies [17.7%]). For bias assessment and mitigation, 61 studies (77.2%) explicitly defined time zero, a key step in reducing immortal time and selection biases, while 26 studies (32.9%) used negative control to assess residual bias and only 2 studies (2.5%) used quantitative bias analysis using E-values. Despite regulatory emphasis on data credibility, systematic data quality assessments appeared in only 5 studies (6.3%).

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, methodological rigor and transparency varied widely, with documented protocols, validated operational definitions, and systematic data quality assessments all uncommon. To improve reproducibility and regulatory credibility, future research should prioritize adopting standardized TTE reporting frameworks, ensure clearly documented protocols, and incorporate data quality assessments.

item.title: Mistrust in Health Care Organizations Among US Adults
item.description:
Importance: Public trust in the health care system has declined for decades. Population-level mistrust and its demographic correlates are well-documented, but because most studies are cross-sectional, little is known about how individuals' mistrust changes over time.

Objective: To examine change in mistrust of health care organizations and to identify sociodemographic factors associated with these changes.

Design, setting, and participants: This longitudinal cohort study used data from a national probability sample of US adults (Ipsos KnowledgePanel) surveyed in 2021 and 2022. Data analysis was from March to April 2026. In 2021, 1449 of 2107 invited individuals (68.8%) responded, and in 2022, 1831 of 2756 (66.4%) individuals responded. Twelve individuals with missing data were excluded.

Exposures: Sociodemographic characteristics including gender, age, education, annual household income, self-rated health, race and ethnicity (categorized as Hispanic, non-Hispanic Black, non-Hispanic White, and other), and political party.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was medical mistrust, assessed with the Medical Mistrust Index, which measures perceptions of health care organizations' honesty, fairness, and motives. Latent class analysis was used to identify classes of mistrust, and multinomial logistic regression was used to estimate associations of sociodemographic characteristics with mistrust class.

Results: Among 1437 participants (mean age, 48.6 [95% CI, 47.4-49.8] years; 51.9% [95% CI, 48.7%-55.1%] women), 4 mistrust statuses were identified at each time point, with similar probability distributions in 2021 and 2022 (strong mistrust: 0.32 vs 0.33; moderate mistrust: 0.33 vs 0.34; neutral: 0.15 vs 0.15; no mistrust: 0.20 vs 0.19). Despite this population-level stability, individual membership changed substantially; the probability of remaining in the same status was 0.26 for strong mistrust, 0.35 for moderate mistrust, 0.18 for neutral, and 0.22 for no mistrust. Non-Hispanic Black participants were less likely than non-Hispanic White participants to move from neutral to no mistrust status (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 0.12; 95% CI, 0.02-0.64), participants with a high school education were less likely than college graduates to move from strong mistrust to neutral (aOR, 0.36; 95% CI, 0.14-0.94), and participants leaning Democratic were more likely than those leaning Republican to move from neutral to no mistrust (aOR, 6.11; 95% CI, 1.20-31.19).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, most US adults reported at least moderate mistrust of health care organizations. Population distributions remained stable, yet most individuals moved between statuses, indicating that mistrust is dynamic rather than fixed. Differences in trust levels across demographic characteristics highlight the need to strengthen trustworthiness in health care systems.

item.title: Gestational Weight Gain and Mortality Among Children in Brazil
item.description:
Importance: Gestational weight gain (GWG) is a key indicator of maternal nutritional status and has been associated with adverse perinatal outcomes. However, evidence of the association of GWG with child mortality remains limited, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

Objective: To examine the association between GWG and mortality among children younger than 5 years in Brazil.

Design, setting, and participants: This population-based cohort study used data from January 1, 2008, to December 31, 2020, from the 100 Million Brazilians Cohort, constructed through linkage of the Live Birth Information System, Food and Nutrition Surveillance System, and Mortality Information System databases, with statistical analyses performed between July and December 2025.

Exposures: GWG was defined as the difference between third trimester and prepregnancy weight and classified as below, within, or above the 2009 US Institute of Medicine guidelines and Brazilian references for GWG.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcome was neonatal mortality, postneonatal mortality, infant mortality, and mortality among children younger than 5 years. Adjusted hazard ratios (AHRs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models controlling for maternal age, education, marital status, prenatal visits, prepregnancy body mass index (BMI), and year of birth. Analyses were stratified by prepregnancy BMI.

Results: Among 792 935 singleton live births from 2008 to 2020 (51.1% boys; 683 656 [86.2%] born to mothers aged 20-34 years), 6105 deaths occurred among children younger than 5 years (0.8%). Compared with GWG within the guidelines, GWG below the guidelines was associated with higher risks of neonatal mortality (AHR, 1.21; 95% CI, 1.11-1.32), postneonatal mortality (AHR, 1.15; 95% CI, 1.04-1.28), infant mortality (AHR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.11-1.27), and mortality among children younger than 5 years (AHR, 1.18; 95% CI, 1.12-1.26). Women with underweight had the greatest AHR for mortality among children younger than 5 years (1.47; 95% CI, 1.10-1.96). GWG above the guidelines was not consistently associated with mortality.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, GWG below the guidelines was associated with increased early-life child mortality, particularly among women with underweight, highlighting the importance of monitoring maternal nutrition during pregnancy among vulnerable populations.

item.title: Mortality From Winter Storm Uri and Texas Power Outages Among Medicare Patients
item.description:
Importance: In February 2021, a severe freeze event and winter storm, together named Winter Storm Uri, caused widespread power outages across Texas, leaving millions vulnerable to record-breaking cold temperatures. The association of these events and the related power outages with population-level health outcomes is unclear.

Objective: To estimate the association of Winter Storm Uri and related power outages with mortality and hospitalizations among Medicare beneficiaries in Texas through a quasi-experimental design.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study used data on a 100% sample of Texas Medicare beneficiaries from 2019 to 2023. The week of Winter Storm Uri was defined as February 14 to February 20, 2021. Statistical analyses were carried out between August 2025 and June 2026.

Exposures: Winter Storm Uri and related power outages in February 2021.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was weekly county-level all-cause mortality in Texas counties among Medicare beneficiaries, compared with the change observed in the same counties in the following year. The secondary outcome was county-level all-cause hospitalizations, measured identically. Difference-in-differences regression models estimated excess mortality and hospitalization rates 4 weeks before and during the week of the storm. Analyses were repeated for the 4 weeks from storm onset. For both outcomes, subgroup analyses were stratified by power outage quartile and by characteristics for vulnerable populations.

Results: The main study sample comprised Texas counties with Medicare beneficiaries in 2021 (n=3 955 190; 50.2% aged 65-74 years; 54.1% female) and the main control sample comprised the same counties in 2022 (n=4 053 788; 49.9% aged 65-74 years; 54.1% female). During the week of Winter Storm Uri, weekly mortality increased by 2.94 (95% CI, 2.12-3.76) deaths per 10 000 beneficiaries. During the 4-week period from storm onset, excess mortality persisted, with 3.08 (95% CI, 2.72-3.44) excess deaths per 10 000 beneficiaries per week. Hospitalizations were not higher during the storm week; however, over the 4-week period from storm onset, hospitalizations were 2.04 (95% CI, 1.30-2.78) higher per 10 000 beneficiaries per week. Although there was widespread storm activity throughout the state, no increase in mortality was observed in counties with the fewest power outages, with 0.66 (95% CI, -2.16 to 3.48) excess deaths per 10 000 beneficiaries per week. Medicare beneficiaries with low income had the highest relative increase in deaths during the storm week, with 5.40 (95% CI, 2.82-7.99) excess deaths per 10 000 beneficiaries.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of Texas Medicare beneficiaries, Winter Storm Uri was associated with excess mortality and hospitalizations, particularly in counties with power outages and among Medicare beneficiaries with low income. These findings highlight the need for targeted public health and policy efforts to protect vulnerable Medicare populations from the growing health consequences of weather-related events.

item.title: Respiratory Syncytial Virus-Related Pediatric Intensive Care Unit Admissions in Children During Their Second RSV Season
item.description:
Importance: Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) hospitalization rates are highest among children younger than 2 years. For certain high-risk children entering their second RSV season, the monoclonal antibody nirsevimab is recommended. Little is known regarding preexisting health conditions as risk factors for RSV-related respiratory failure in children during their second RSV season.

Objective: To describe children admitted to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for severe RSV by classifying them by their nirsevimab eligibility status and preexisting health conditions, and comparing their demographic and clinical characteristics.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study analyzed US children aged 8 to 23 months admitted to the PICU in 30 pediatric hospitals in the 2023 to 2024 and 2024 to 2025 RSV seasons. All children had an RSV-positive result from a respiratory sample and received respiratory support with high-flow nasal cannula, noninvasive ventilation, or invasive mechanical ventilation. Analyses were based on the US criteria for second-season nirsevimab eligibility as recommended in August 2023.

Exposure: Preexisting health conditions potentially associated with increased risk of severe RSV disease. Patients were classified into 4 mutually exclusive groups of eligibility status and preexisting health conditions: (1) met nirsevimab eligibility criteria, (2) with other identified RSV risk conditions (with some evidence of increased risk for severe RSV), (3) with other preexisting conditions, and (4) with no preexisting conditions.

Main outcomes and measures: Patient demographic characteristics and level of respiratory support received were compared by level of preexisting health conditions.

Results: A total of 574 children (median [IQR] age, 1.2 [1.1-1.5] years; 317 males [55.2%]) were included. Overall, 47 patients (8.2%) met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria, 76 (13.2%) had other identified RSV risk conditions, 96 (16.7%) had other preexisting conditions, and 355 (61.8%) had no preexisting conditions. A higher proportion of children who met nirsevimab eligibility criteria required invasive mechanical ventilation vs children with other identified RSV risk conditions, those with other preexisting health conditions, or those with no preexisting health conditions (40.4% [19 of 47] vs 17.1% [13 of 76], 10.4% [10 of 96], 5.9% [21 of 355]; P for trend <.001).

Conclusions and relevance: Among children admitted to the PICU for severe RSV, 8.2% met the nirsevimab eligibility criteria and 13.2% had other identified RSV risk conditions. These findings might help inform future deliberations regarding second RSV season recommendations for nirsevimab eligibility in the US.

item.title: Milk Fat Globule Membrane-Enriched Formula and Cognition Among Formula-Fed Infants: A Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: The absence of milk fat globule membrane (MFGM) in infant formula may contribute to the differences between breastfed and formula-fed infants.

Objective: To test whether MFGM-enriched infant formula benefits cognitive development of exclusively formula-fed infants.

Design, setting, and participants: This clinician-blinded, researcher-blinded, and participant-blinded randomized clinical trial of exclusively formula-fed infants with a reference group (exclusively breastfed) included full-term singleton infants under 2 months of age, who were recruited from the community (May 2020 to April 2022). Follow-up was completed in June 2024 and analyses completed in September 2025.

Interventions: Randomized infants received either MFGM-enriched formula (treatment group: 0.55 g per 100.00 g of MFGM component phospholipid from MFGM Lipid 100 [New Zealand Milk Products, Fonterra Co-Operative Group Limited]) or standard formula (control group: no added MFGM, 0.29 g per 100.00 g of MFGM component phospholipid) from randomization to 12 months of age.

Main outcomes and measures: The Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, 4th Edition scales for cognitive, language, motor, emotional, and behavioral development, in which the mean (SD) score is 100 (15), with scores below 85 classified as delayed, were administered at ages 12 months and 24 months; the primary outcome was the 12-month cognitive score. Caregivers reported health, language, development, growth, safety, and tolerance.

Results: There were 416 randomized formula-fed infants (mean [SD] age, 36.6 [11.5] days; 209 males [50.2%]) and 204 reference group infants. Primary outcome data were available for 382 randomized infants (91.8%), including 193 (93.2%) of 207 in the treatment group and 189 (90.4%) of 209 in the control group. The mean (SD) 12-month cognitive scores in the treatment group (100.1 [11.9]) and control group (99.4 [14.1]) were not significant (adjusted mean difference, 0.68 [95% CI, -1.94 to 3.31]; P = .61). There was a significantly lower risk of delayed cognition (<85) at age 12 months in the treatment group compared with the control group (10.0 [4.8%] vs 24.1 [11.5%]; adjusted relative risk, 0.42 [95% CI, 0.20-0.90]; P = .03), and the mean (SD) language scores at age 24 months were higher in the treatment group compared with the control group (93.0 [16.3] vs 90.0 [16.6]; adjusted mean difference, 2.87 [95% CI, 0.10-5.65]; P = .04), although this difference was not statistically significant after controlling for caregiver educational level. Other secondary developmental outcomes, as well as growth and safety outcomes, were mostly not significant.

Conclusions and relevance: In this randomized clinical trial of MFGM-supplemented formula compared with standard formula among nonbreastfed infants, mean cognitive scores were not improved, although a reduction in the number of infants with cognitive delay is worthy of further investigation.

Trial registration: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry identifier: ACTRN12620000552987.

item.title: Metastatic Prostate Cancer Treatment Variation in Veterans
item.description:
Importance: Not all men with metastatic castration-sensitive prostate cancer (mCSPC) receive the recommended combination therapy of androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) plus an androgen receptor pathway inhibitor (ARPI) and/or chemotherapy.

Objective: To determine factors associated with combination therapy use among veterans with mCSPC in the national Veterans Health Administration (VHA) system.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study included US veterans diagnosed with mCSPC between January 1, 2023, through December 31, 2024, who were followed up through June 30, 2025. National multicenter data were obtained from the VHA electronic health record, community care settings (private care paid with VHA benefits), and Medicare. All included veterans were identified through a validated natural language processing algorithm, were followed up in the VHA for at least 2 years prior to their metastatic diagnosis, were provided ADT within the first 6 months of diagnosis, and received no prostate cancer-directed therapy in the year prior to diagnosis.

Exposure: Clinical factors (eg, comorbidities, frailty, prostate cancer burden at diagnosis) and nonclinical factors (eg, annual household income, neighborhood disadvantage) were investigated to determine their association with the outcome.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was receipt of combination therapy (ie, ADT plus ARPI [abiraterone, enzalutamide, apalutamide, darolutamide] and/or docetaxel) vs ADT alone. Information on these treatments was obtained through pharmacy records. Multilevel logistic regression models were used and marginal predicted probabilities were reported to determine the associations of factors with receipt of combination therapy. Variation among VHA facilities was reported.

Results: A total of 4023 veterans (mean [SD] age, 75.3 [8.0] years) met eligibility criteria. Of these patients, 2339 (58.1%) had de novo metastatic disease, while 1684 (41.9%) had recurrent disease. Overall, 2564 patients (63.7%) received combination therapy. In adjusted analyses, older veterans (eg, aged 85-89 years: predicted probability, -14.1 [95% CI, -20.5 to -8.2] percentage points [pp]) and veterans with more comorbidities (eg, congestive heart failure: predicted probability, -7.5 [95% CI, -12.9 to -2.5] pp) were less likely to receive combination therapy. Annual household income and neighborhood disadvantage were not associated with receipt of combination therapy. Patients treated by urologists were less likely to receive combination therapy than patients treated by hematologist-oncologists (predicted probability, -23.7 [95% CI, -27.4 to -19.6] pp). Use of combination therapy ranged from 34% to 78% among VHA facilities.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of veterans with de novo and recurrent mCSPC, receipt of combination therapy was high; annual household income and neighborhood disadvantage had no association with treatment use. The study findings suggest that the region where a veteran lives, the facility where they receive care, and the type of cancer specialist they see are factors of the variation in combination therapy use that need further exploration.

item.title: Bystander CPR Type and Outcomes After Pediatric Out-of-Hospital Cardiac Arrest
item.description:
Importance: Compression-only cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CO-CPR) has been widely promoted to encourage bystander intervention in out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA), but long-term trends in bystander CPR and the associations between CPR type and outcomes in pediatric OHCA remain unclear.

Objective: To evaluate temporal trends in bystander CPR type and the associations with clinical outcomes among children with OHCA in Japan.

Design, setting, and participants: This cohort study included patients aged 17 years or younger with known receipt of bystander CPR documented in the nationwide All-Japan Utstein Registry from January 1, 2005, to December 31, 2023. Data analysis was performed from November 24, 2025, to September 2, 2026, including additional analyses conducted during the revision process.

Exposures: Bystander CPR was categorized as rescue-breathing CPR (RB-CPR), CO-CPR, or no bystander CPR.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate; secondary outcomes were 30-day survival rate and prehospital return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC). Temporal trends were assessed with multinomial logistic regression, and associations between CPR type and outcomes were evaluated using modified Poisson regression with robust variance estimation, with CO-CPR serving as the reference.

Results: Among 26 785 pediatric patients with OHCA (median [IQR] age, 2.0 [0-12] years; 16 254 males [60.7%]), 6543 (24.4%) received RB-CPR, 9112 (34.0%) received CO-CPR, and 11 130 (41.6%) received no bystander CPR. The adjusted probability of CO-CPR increased from 14.6% (95% CI, 13.1%-16.1%) in 2005 to 55.1% (95% CI, 52.5%-57.6%) in 2023, whereas RB-CPR declined from 41.7% (95% CI, 39.7%-43.7%) to 10.4% (95% CI, 8.7%-12.1%). The adjusted probability of receiving no bystander CPR plateaued at approximately 35.0% after 2013. Neurologically favorable 30-day survival rate occurred in 3.6% receiving no bystander CPR, 9.5% receiving CO-CPR, and 16.0% receiving RB-CPR. Compared with CO-CPR, RB-CPR was associated with a higher 30-day neurologically favorable survival rate (adjusted risk ratio [ARR], 1.71; 95% CI, 1.57-1.86), 30-day survival rate (ARR, 1.51; 95% CI, 1.42-1.61), and prehospital ROSC (ARR, 1.62; 95% CI, 1.51-1.75), whereas receipt of no bystander CPR was associated with lower probabilities of these outcomes.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of children with OHCA, increasing CO-CPR use coincided with declining RB-CPR but not with further reductions in untreated arrests after 2013. No bystander CPR was associated with worse outcomes compared with CO-CPR and RB-CPR. RB-CPR had more favorable outcomes than CO-CPR, supporting the continued importance of rescue breathing in pediatric resuscitation.

item.title: Commercial Health Care Prices and Medical Debt in the US
item.description:
Importance: Medical debt remains a major source of financial strain for US households. Although commercial health care prices vary substantially across markets, little is known about how these prices are associated with medical debt.

Objective: To examine the association between changes in commercial to Medicare price ratios and changes in medical debt in collections across US local markets.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study used data from multiple geographic areas (referred to hereinafter as geozips) in the US. Commercial to Medicare price ratio data were obtained from FAIR Health claims for 2020 and 2022 to 2023, and medical debt outcomes were measured using the Urban Institute Credit Panel in August 2020 and August 2023. Analyses were conducted between October 2025 and August 2026 at the geozip level using a 2-period ecologic first-difference model.

Exposures: Changes in commercial to Medicare price ratios for professional, outpatient, and inpatient services.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the change in the share of adults with with medical debt in collections exceeding $500.

Results: The sample included 479 geozips in the US. A 1-unit increase in the professional commercial to Medicare price ratio was associated with a 4.3-percentage point increase (0.043; 95% CI, 0.027-0.060; P < .001) in the share of adults with medical debt in collections above $500. Changes in the inpatient and outpatient price ratios were not statistically associated with medical debt in collections exceeding $500.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of US geozips from 2020 to 2023, increases in commercial to Medicare price ratios for professional services were associated with increases in medical debt in collections, whereas changes in inpatient and outpatient price ratios were not. These findings suggest that commercial price increases in services more directly tied to patient cost sharing coincide with increased financial hardship.

item.title: Prevalence of Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy Without Contact Sport Repetitive Head Impact Exposure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
item.description:
Importance: A pooled baseline prevalence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in populations without repetitive head impact (RHI) exposure is needed to contextualize prevalence in other cohorts.

Objective: To estimate the pooled prevalence of CTE in populations without documented contact sport-based RHI exposure.

Data sources: PubMed and Embase were searched from inception through February 23, 2026, using terms for CTE, prevalence, epidemiology, and neuropathology.

Study selection: Studies reporting CTE prevalence in cohorts without documented contact sport RHI history were included and classified by ascertainment rigor into a primary group with verified absence of contact sport RHI or a secondary unscreened reference cohort. Studies were excluded for cohort overlap or for RHI-linked comorbid conditions (eg, epilepsy).

Data extraction and synthesis: Data were independently extracted by 2 authors, with discrepancy resolved by a third. Risk of bias and quality were assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute checklist. Pooled prevalence was calculated using a random-effects model with restricted maximum likelihood estimation. Heterogeneity (I2 and τ2) and robustness (leave-one-out sensitivity analysis) were assessed.

Main outcomes and measures: Confirmed CTE in individuals without documented contact sport RHI history was estimated using pooled prevalence and 95% CIs.

Results: Twelve cohort studies (4421 individuals; weighted mean age at death, 75.1 years; 2481 male [56.1%]) were identified. item.title: Firearm Homicide Surges From 1979 to 2023
item.description:
Importance: US firearm homicide rates surged twice in the past 35 years. Better understanding of such surges could aid prevention.

Objective: To compare the demographic and geographic distribution of surge deaths and examine state-level correlates of surge severity across the 1985-1993 and 2014-2021 firearm homicide surge periods.

Design, setting, and participants: This serial cross-sectional study obtained homicide counts from 1979 to 2023, stratified by race, sex, age group, county urbanicity, and state, from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The firearm homicide surge periods 1985 to 1993 and 2014 to 2021 were analyzed. Although both Black and Hispanic people in the US bear a disproportionate burden of firearm homicide, Hispanic ethnicity was not consistently coded in mortality records over the study period (1979-2023); thus, a single categorization of Black or other race was used. Data analyses were conducted in April 2025 to September 2026.

Exposure: Presurge levels and presurge-to-surge changes in state measures of drug-market violence, proxy measures for firearm availability and use, economic strength, social or economic disadvantage, urban concentration, social or economic disruption, and policing capacity.

Main outcomes and measures: Annualized firearm homicide surge rates (deaths per 100 000 population, above presurge rates). Correlations between state-level surge rates and proxy measures were calculated.

Results: The 2014-2021 surge produced an estimated mean (SE) of 31 489 (509) firearm surge deaths, with a mean (SE) annualized rate of 1.20 (0.02) deaths per 100 000 population per year above presurge rates. In the 1985-1993 surge, the mean (SE) number of firearm surge deaths was 24 276 (580), with a mean (SE) annualized rate of 1.09 (0.03) deaths per 100 000 population. Both surges were driven entirely by firearm homicide, as non-firearm homicides declined over both periods. Deaths of young urban Black males (aged 15-24 years) accounted for 47% of 1985-1993 surge deaths but only 14% of the 2014-2021 surge. Compared with the 1985-1993 surge, during the 2014-2021 surge, the mean (SE) firearm homicide surge rates increased for females (0.15 [0.02] vs 0.38 [0.01]), people of races other than Black (0.22 [0.02] vs 0.48 [0.01]), and rural residents (0.13 [0.04] vs 0.83 [0.03]). Across US states, the 1985-1993 surge correlated with crack cocaine market activity (r = 0.44; 95% CI, 0.19-0.64), while the 2014-2021 surge correlated with presurge firearm availability proxies (r = 0.68 [95% CI, 0.50-0.81] for value of stolen firearms per capita) and COVID-19-related death rates (r = 0.61; 95% CI, 0.40-0.76). Across both eras, higher state-level surge rates correlated with social or economic disadvantage, including premature mortality, poverty rates, lower employment, and household instability.

Conclusions and relevance: In this serial cross-sectional study of US firearm homicide mortality, both the 2014-2021 surge, which was substantially larger and more demographically and geographically dispersed, and the 1985-1993 surge were associated with distinct proximal correlates but disproportionately affected states with broader structural vulnerabilities. Proximal drivers of rapid increases in homicide rates may exacerbate long-standing population vulnerabilities.

item.title: Multicomponent Lifestyle Intervention and Brain Aging: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Multicomponent lifestyle interventions show promise for promoting cognitive health, but their effects on clinically established brain aging markers among individuals with amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI) are unclear. Intervention adherence may influence intervention efficacy.

Objectives: To evaluate the association of combined aerobic exercise and cognitive training (ACT) with brain aging markers and to explore the role of intervention adherence.

Design, setting, and participants: This secondary analysis of a phase 2, single-blind, 2 × 2 factorial randomized clinical trial with data collection lasting up to 18 months per participant was conducted at 3 academic research facilities between April 1, 2018, and July 17, 2024. Among 911 individuals screened, 146 participants with aMCI were randomized. Data were analyzed from October 10, 2025, to January 8, 2026.

Interventions: The ACT intervention was compared with 3 other intervention arms during a 6-month period, including speed-of-processing training (SOP), cycling, and mental leisure activities plus stretching (MS).

Main outcomes and measures: Alzheimer disease signature for cortical thickness (ADSCT) and natural log-transformed white matter hyperintensity (ln-WMH) were assessed at baseline, post intervention, and at the 12- and 18-month follow-ups. Outcome-specific modified intention-to-treat analyses used 100 forward-only multiple imputations and age-, sex-, and site-adjusted linear mixed-effects models with a participant random intercept. Visit-specific complete-case and attendance analyses used participants observed at baseline and the relevant follow-up.

Results: Among 146 randomized participants (mean [SD] age, 73.8 [5.7] years), 75 (51.4%) were male. A total of 144 participants had baseline ADSCT and 141 had baseline ln-WMH measurements. In primary analyses, compared with ACT, SOP was associated with greater worsening in 18-month ADSCT change (B = -0.060 [95% CI, -0.117 to -0.004] mm; P = .04), and MS was associated with greater 12-month worsening (B = -0.066 [95% CI, -0.122 to -0.011] mm; P = .02). No primary ln-WMH contrast was significant. In visit-specific complete cases, cycling was associated with greater 18-month ln-WMH progression than ACT (B = 0.452 [95% CI, 0.131-0.772] natural log units; P = .006). Exploratory within-ACT analyses linked each of 10 additional sessions to greater postintervention ADSCT change (B = 0.022 [95% CI, 0.002-0.042] mm; P = .03), but not ln-WMH change.

Conclusions and relevance: In this secondary analysis of a randomized clinical trial of older adults with aMCI, ACT was associated with more favorable ADSCT change than SOP at 18 months and MS at 12 months. No primary ln-WMH contrast was significant. Attendance findings were post randomization and exploratory. Larger confirmatory trials are needed to verify these findings.

item.title: Sleep-Wake Cycle Profiles and Incident Dementia and Cognitive Decline in Older Adults
item.description:
Importance: Sleep-wake cycle (SWC) disruptions are common in patients with dementia and potentially also in the preclinical phase of the disease. Accelerometers allow objective measures of multiple SWC dimensions: rest-activity rhythm (RAR), daytime activity, sleep, and chronotype, but these dimensions are rarely examined together.

Objective: This study examined the association of SWC profiles, incorporating the 4 SWC dimensions, with incident dementia and cognitive decline.

Design, setting, and participants: Prospective, UK population-based cohort study based on accelerometer data from the 2012 to 2013 wave of the Whitehall II cohort study, with a median (IQR) follow-up of 12.3 (12.0-12.7) years. Statistical analyses were conducted from June 2025 to March 2026. Participants were dementia-free aged 60 years or older with valid accelerometer data and covariates at baseline.

Exposure: Nine SWC profiles derived from 36 SWC metrics.

Main outcomes and measures: Incident dementia cases until March 2025 were retrieved from electronic health records. Cognitive tests were administered in 2012 to 2013, 2015 to 2016, and 2019 to 2022 and each test score was standardized based on 2012 to 2013 data and all tests averaged to derive a global cognitive z score.

Results: Among 3973 participants (median [IQR] age = 68.4 [64.7 to 74.0] years; 26% women), 379 dementia cases were recorded during a median 12.3-year follow-up. Compared with participants with robust RAR (high level and amplitude, stable, not fragmented), light-intensity physical activity (PA) and good sleep (profile 3), those with poorer RAR (low level and amplitude, unstable, fragmented) along with low PA and poor sleep (profile 7), or with high level and low amplitude RAR and restless sleep (profile 8) had higher dementia risk (hazard ratio, 1.94 [95% CI, 1.32 to 2.84], and 1.96 [95% CI, 1.27 to 3.03], respectively). In analyses on cognitive decline (3806 participants), profile 7 as well as the most sedentary profile with the poorest RAR (profile 9) had faster 10-year cognitive decline (-0.14 [95% CI, -0.26 to -0.02]) and -0.28 [95% CI, -0.44 to -0.13], respectively). Cognitive outcomes in participants with robust RAR and higher PA were similar, irrespective of sleep.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 3973 older adults, consideration of all SWC dimensions was important in identifying profiles associated with cognitive outcomes; further studies are needed to evaluate whether SWC interventions reduce the risk or delay onset of dementia.

item.title: Cost-Effectiveness of Alcohol Use Disorder Treatment for Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease
item.description:
Importance: Alcohol-associated liver disease (ALD) is a leading cause of liver-related mortality and liver transplant. Combined behavioral interventions (CBI) and medications for alcohol use disorder (MAUD) are underutilized. Thus, it is critical to identify optimal therapeutic and cost-effective windows for CBI and MAUD in patients with ALD at earlier fibrosis stages.

Objective: To evaluate the cost-effectiveness of naltrexone and CBI in preventing cirrhosis in patients with ALD compared with no treatment.

Design, setting, and participants: This economic evaluation used a Markov state-transition model simulating lifetime disease progression and health care costs associated with ALD. The simulated patient cohort began at 45 years of age with active AUD and stage 3 fibrosis (F3) and could experience progression to compensated or decompensated cirrhosis.

Exposure: All patients were assumed to complete a 16-week course of naltrexone along with 52 weeks of CBI.

Main outcomes and measures: Primary outcomes included total health care cost, quality-adjusted life-years (QALYs), and incremental cost-effectiveness ratios. Secondary outcomes included liver-related mortality and progression to compensated and decompensated cirrhosis. Scenario and sensitivity analyses were performed to determine outcomes at earlier stages and with varied cost and model parameters.

Results: Without intervention, 61% of the cohort died from liver-related causes, 88% developed compensated cirrhosis, and 66% of those experienced progression to decompensated cirrhosis, with a lifetime cost of $79 799 per person. With treatment initiated at F3, liver-related mortality was reduced to 58%, lifetime compensated cirrhosis to 87%, and lifetime progression to decompensated cirrhosis to 62%, with a lifetime cost of $78 673. The treatment strategy dominated because the lifetime costs were lower and more QALYs were gained when compared with untreated natural history. Treatment was preferred in sensitivity analyses at relapse rates to 100% and adherence greater than 0%, in scenario analyses when treatment was initiated at stages F2 and F1, and for the models including societal and AUD costs.

Conclusions and relevance: In this economic evaluation of AUD treatment for patients with ALD, treating patients with ALD with naltrexone and CBI at F3 saved cost and was more effective than no treatment, reducing progression to compensated and decompensated cirrhosis. The results remained true at stages F1 and F2 fibrosis and when considering the societal costs and the costs of AUD. Future studies should include prospective evaluations of screening strategies combined with early treatment, as many patients are diagnosed at advanced stages of ALD.

item.title: Clinician Acceptance of Large Language Model-Generated Discharge Summaries
item.description:
Importance: Hospital discharge summaries are essential for continuity of care, but fragmented electronic health record (EHR) data can compromise their quality and safety. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for clinical documentation tasks despite limited evidence regarding their performance in health care settings compared with the current standard of care.

Objective: To evaluate clinician acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries derived from EHRs compared with routine clinician-written summaries.

Design, setting, and participants: In this retrospective comparative effectiveness study using a prespecified noninferiority framework, acceptability of LLM-generated discharge summaries was compared with clinician-authored discharge summaries. Admission records from 5 London hospitals for September 1, 2022, to September 30, 2023, were evaluated against the full admission record by practicing physicians. Admissions were eligible only if the clinician-authored discharge summary contained identifiable clinical summary, plan and requested actions, and information given sections. Data analysis was conducted from July 2025 to February 2026.

Intervention: LLM-generated summaries were produced using GPT-4o mini (July 18, 2024 release; OpenAI) and a clinician-codesigned prompt.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was clinician signoff with no or minor edits, derived from 2 sequential questions: (1) whether the reviewer would sign the summary and (2) whether no, minor, or major edits were required. A 5-percentage-point noninferiority margin was prespecified. Secondary outcomes assessed accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, poor; 2, fair; 3, good; 4, very good; and 5, excellent) and potential harmfulness of missing or incorrect information (using a 5-point Likert scale: 1, no harm; 2, minor harm; 3, moderate harm; 4, high harm; and 5, extremely high harm).

Results: The study sample included 1294 (649 clinician-authored and 645 LLM-generated) unique case discharge summaries that were evaluated against the full admission record by 12 practicing physicians. Case patients had a median age of 46.0 years (IQR, 26.2-69.8 years), 733 (56.6%) were assigned female at birth, and the median length of stay was 3.0 days (IQR, 1.0-7.0 days). The absolute difference in model-estimated probability of signoff with no or minor edits (LLM generated minus clinician authored) was 22.2 percentage points (95% CI, 19.0-27.5 percentage points); the lower bound exceeded the prespecified noninferiority margin of -5 percentage points, demonstrating noninferiority. LLM-generated summaries received higher ratings for accuracy, completeness, tone, and clarity (adjusted risk differences for scores ≥4 ranged from 19.4 [95% CI, 14.8-24.1] to 29.1 [95% CI, 25.1-33.6] percentage points; all 95% CIs excluded 0). LLM-generated summaries also had a lower proportion of cases rated 3 or greater for potential harm on the clinical summary and plan and requested actions sections (140 of 534 [26.2%] and 124 of 462 [26.8%]) compared with clinician-authored summaries (271 of 601 [45.1%] and 278 of 540 [51.5%]).

Conclusions and relevance: In this study, LLM-generated discharge summaries met the current standard of care, representing a promising early use case for generative artificial intelligence in health care with close clinician oversight.

item.title: Timing of Antenatal Care, Stillbirth, and Infant Mortality in Migrant Mothers in Australia
item.description:
Importance: Timely antenatal care (ANC) reduces pregnancy risks, yet the association between delayed ANC and stillbirth or infant mortality among migrant mothers in Australia has not previously been investigated.

Objective: To examine whether delayed ANC is associated with higher stillbirth and infant mortality among Australia-born compared with migrant mothers.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective cohort study assessed births to non-Indigenous mothers in New South Wales from January 1, 2002, to December 31, 2020, followed up to infant age of 1 year. Mothers were categorized as Australia-born, migrant from English-speaking country (ESM), or migrant from non-English-speaking country (non-ESM). Data were analyzed between August 2025 and June 2026.

Exposures: Timing of first ANC, defined as 12 weeks or earlier, 13 to 19 weeks, 20 weeks or later, or no ANC.

Main outcomes and measures: The main outcome was stillbirth (at ≥20 weeks) and infant mortality (at prehospital discharge, posthospital discharge, or 1 year). Adjusted relative risks (ARRs) were estimated using Poisson regression models, stratified by migration group.

Results: This study included 1 720 033 births (median [IQR] maternal age, 31.2 [27.4-34.8] years; 884 235 male infants [51.4%]), including 1 132 193 (65.8%) to Australia-born, 116 026 (6.7%) to ESM, and 471 814 (27.4%) to non-ESM mothers. Late ANC (>12 weeks) was more common in non-ESM mothers (190 338 [40.3%]) than Australia-born (334 790 [29.6%]) or ESM (41 029 [35.4%]) mothers. In cross-group comparisons, non-ESM mother status was associated with higher risk of adverse outcomes regardless of ANC timing. Compared with Australia-born mothers with early ANC (≤12 weeks), a higher risk of stillbirth (ARR, 1.25; 95% CI, 1.18-1.33) and 1-year (ARR, 1.32; 95% CI, 1.22-1.44), predischarge (ARR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.25-1.54), and postdischarge (ARR, 1.19; 95% CI, 1.03-1.37) infant mortality was observed in non-ESM mothers accessing ANC by 12 weeks. Similar risk patterns were observed in non-ESM mothers with late ANC. In within-group comparisons, among Australia-born mothers, each category of delayed ANC was associated with higher risk. No ANC was associated with the highest risks across all maternal groups for stillbirth and 1-year infant mortality. For non-ESM mothers, late ANC (≥20 weeks) was associated with a lower risk of predischarge mortality (ARR, 0.75; 95% CI, 0.61-0.92) but a higher risk of postdischarge mortality (ARR, 1.30; 95% CI, 1.02-1.65).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 1.72 million births, higher risks of stillbirths and infant mortalities were observed in non-ESM mothers regardless of ANC timing, warranting further investigation.

item.title: Neighborhood Deprivation and Developmental Concerns Across Early Childhood
item.description:
Importance: Neighborhood deprivation is an important environmental context for understanding child development and has been linked in extensive prior work with physical and cognitive outcomes. However, neighborhood deprivation is understudied in relation to socioemotional development in early childhood, a critical period for prevention and intervention.

Objective: To examine prospective associations between neighborhood deprivation and children's socioemotional development from infancy to preschool age and to test whether associations differ by race.

Design, setting, and participants: In this longitudinal cohort study, participants were mother-child dyads with available neighborhood and socioemotional assessment data who were recruited in April 2020 from the greater Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, area as part of a longitudinal cohort within a large health system. Assessments were conducted at child ages 1, 2, and 4 years. Data collection started in June 2021 for children aged 1 year and in May 2024 for children aged 4 years and ended in March 2025.

Exposure: A composite neighborhood deprivation index derived from objective US census-based measures linked to participants' residential addresses, including the Child Opportunity Index, Area Deprivation Index, Social Vulnerability Index, and Heat Vulnerability Index.

Main outcomes and measures: Parent-reported developmental concerns from Ages and Stages Questionnaires: Social-Emotional, Second Edition (ASQ:SE-2) scores at each age and electronic health record (EHR) data on developmental or behavioral diagnoses.

Results: The analytic sample included 249 mother-child dyads; 125 children (50.2%) were female. A total of 130 households (52.2%) were included in the White group and 118 (47.8%) in the Black or multiracial group. Greater neighborhood deprivation was associated with more parent-reported socioemotional concerns (β = 0.29 [95% CI, 0.20-0.38]; P < .001), independent of family income and maternal anxiety. Children from more deprived neighborhoods had increased odds of being referred for monitoring or intervention (odds ratio [OR], 2.43 [95% CI, 1.05-5.64]; P = .04). A similar pattern was observed for developmental or behavioral diagnoses in children's electronic health records (OR, 1.40 [95% CI, 1.01-2.01]; P = .050). The magnitude of these associations was greater among children from Black or multiracial households, who lived in significantly more deprived neighborhoods than children from White households (χ21 = 304.62; P < .001).

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study, neighborhood deprivation was associated with worse socioemotional functioning across early childhood, above and beyond family-level factors. Children from Black or multiracial compared with White households lived in neighborhoods with greater disadvantage, emphasizing underlying structural inequities and the importance of community-level investment and equitable urban planning to support early developmental health and equity.

item.title: Multilevel Mobility Intervention and Life-Space Mobility in Older Hospitalized Medical Patients: A Cluster Randomized Clinical Trial
item.description:
Importance: Low mobility is common during an acute hospitalization and is associated with adverse outcomes, such as loss of independence and death. Previous interventions that were successful in increasing hospital mobility required resources that are not available in everyday clinical practice, limiting their scalability.

Objective: To assess whether the theory-informed Intervention to Increase Mobility in Older Hospitalized Medical Patients (INTOMOB) improves life-space mobility at 30 days in older hospitalized medical patients.

Design, setting, and participants: This is a multicenter, parallel, partially blinded, cluster randomized clinical superiority trial, with randomization at the hospital ward level and 180-day follow-up. Patients were recruited between October 2023 and January 2025 at acute general internal medicine wards of 3 Swiss hospitals. Main eligibility criteria were age 60 years or older, living in the community, and planned hospital stay 3 or more days.

Intervention: The intervention was compared with standard of care and included booklets and videos for patients, health care professional training, and posters in the wards.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was life-space mobility at 30 days, a measure of how far and often a person moves within their environment, from bedroom to beyond their town (range, 0-120 points, with higher scores denoting greater mobility). Secondary outcomes included physical activity during hospitalization, new institutionalizations (ie, transition to nursing home), and quality of life. For time-to-event outcomes, Cox models with cluster-robust SEs were used. Multinomial logistic regression with robust SEs was used for categorical outcomes.

Results: Of 1334 eligible patients, 383 (median [IQR] age, 75 [68 to 81] years; 234 male [61.1%]) agreed to participate and were randomized to 12 clusters (183 patients [47.8%] in the intervention group and 200 patients [52.2%] in the control group). The primary outcome was available for 327 patients (85.4%). The median (IQR) length of stay was 5 (3 to 7) days. Life-space mobility at 30 days was not significantly different between control and intervention groups (adjusted difference, 0.67 points; 95% CI, -4.35 to 5.68 points). There were no serious adverse events potentially related to the intervention. There was no consistent statistically significant difference in any other secondary outcomes.

Conclusions and relevance: The INTOMOB intervention did not result in a significantly improved short-term life-space mobility or other clinical outcomes. However, the feasibility of the INTOMOB intervention provides a foundation for future mobility interventions aiming to improve both effectiveness and applicability in everyday clinical practice.

item.description:
Importance: Trimodality therapy (TMT) is an established bladder-preservation approach for muscle-invasive bladder cancer (MIBC). Accurate clinical staging remains challenging and may affect patient selection, trial design, and interpretation of outcomes.

Objective: To describe the design, accrual, and baseline characteristics of the Phase III Randomized Trial of Concurrent Chemoradiotherapy With or Without Atezolizumab in Localized Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer (INTACT) trial and evaluate agreement between site-reported and centrally reviewed clinical stage and the prevalence of high-risk disease features.

Design, setting, and participants: INTACT is a phase 3 randomized clinical trial that enrolled patients with localized MIBC (stage cT2-T4aN0M0) at 136 US sites between April 2019 and March 2025. For this analysis, 243 patients with available source documentation were randomly selected by the SWOG Statistical Center for central clinical staging review.

Interventions: Patients were randomized to physician's choice of concurrent chemotherapy (cisplatin, gemcitabine, or 5-fluorouracil and mitomycin C) and radiotherapy (bladder only or small pelvis; 64-64.8 Gy), with or without atezolizumab (1200 mg intravenously every 3 weeks for 9 cycles).

Main outcomes and measures: The trial's primary end point is 3-year bladder-intact event-free survival, which is not reported in this analysis. Outcomes for the present analysis included trial accrual, clinical stage distribution, agreement between site-reported stage and the initial independent central reviewer, and prevalence of predefined high-risk features (carcinoma in situ, unilateral hydronephrosis, or tumor >5 cm). Agreement was assessed using Cohen κ and directional disagreement using the McNemar test.

Results: Among 485 randomized patients, the median (IQR) age was 73.8 (37.6-93.6) years, 384 (79.2%) were male, 16 (3.3%) were Asian, 33 (6.8%) were Black, and 419 (86.4%) were White. Site investigators classified 398 (82.1%) as stage cT2 and 87 (17.9%) as stage cT3 or T4a. Among 243 patients selected for central review, 201 (82.7%) had site-reported stage cT2 disease and 42 (17.3%) had stage cT3 or T4a disease. Agreement between site-reported stage and the initial independent central reviewer was moderate (κ = 0.48; 95% CI, 0.34-0.62). Of 201 site-reported stage cT2 cases, 24 (11.9%) were assigned stage cT3 or T4a by the central reviewer; of 42 site-reported stage cT3 or T4a cases, 15 (35.7%) were assigned stage cT2. Among patients with site-reported stage cT2 disease, 113 (56.2%) had at least 1 high-risk feature. Overall, 155 of 243 patients (63.8%) had at least 1 high-risk feature.

Conclusions and relevance: In this phase 3 randomized clinical trial, a pragmatic design facilitated accrual of 485 patients to a US bladder-preservation trial. Clinical staging showed moderate agreement between site investigators and independent central review, and more than half of patients classified as stage cT2 had additional high-risk features. These findings support standardized collection of clinical staging and high-risk disease characteristics in future bladder-preservation trials.

item.title: Nationwide Assessment of Trends, Characteristics, and Outcomes of Pregnancy for Cancer Survivors
item.description:
Importance: Cancer survivors are individuals with a diagnosis of malignant neoplasm, either living with (ie, current cancer survivors) or free of (ie, past cancer survivors) cancer. As the prevalence of cancer survivors of reproductive age increases worldwide, assessment of pregnancy characteristics and outcomes among past cancer survivors is important.

Objective: To assess the temporal trends, clinical and obstetric characteristics, and maternal morbidity at delivery among current and past cancer survivors.

Design, setting, and participants: This nationwide cross-sectional study used National Inpatient Sample data for hospital deliveries from 2016 to 2023. Analyses were conducted from April to May 2026.

Exposure: A prior or current diagnosis of cancer at hospital delivery, with individuals classified as being a past cancer survivor, a current cancer survivor, or an individual without a cancer diagnosis.

Main outcome and measure: The primary outcome was severe maternal morbidity at delivery, assessed with multivariable generalized linear models with a Poisson distribution.

Results: Among 28 360 443 hospital deliveries, there were 106 740 (0.4%) hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors, 21 975 (<0.1%) for current cancer survivors, and 28 231 728 (99.5%) without a cancer diagnosis. The median (IQR) maternal age at delivery was 33 (29-36), 32 (27-36), and 29 (25-33) years among past cancer survivors, current cancer survivors, and individuals without a cancer diagnosis, respectively. During the 8-year study period, hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors increased from 30.1 to 45.6 per 10 000 hospital deliveries (average annual percentage change [AAPC] = 6.3% [95% CI, 5.1%-7.9%]), whereas hospital deliveries for current cancer survivors were unchanged (7.0 to 7.4 per 10 000 hospital deliveries; AAPC = 0.2% [95% CI, -2.8% to 3.7%]). Most hospital deliveries (57.6%) for past cancer survivors were full-term, whereas only 39.6% were full-term for current cancer survivors. Compared with the no cancer group, the severe maternal morbidity rate was higher for the past cancer survivor group (11.9 vs 6.8 per 1000 hospital deliveries; adjusted incidence rate ratio [IRR], 1.45 [95% CI, 1.37-1.53]) and for the current cancer survivor group (48.2 vs 6.8 per 1000 hospital deliveries; adjusted IRR, 3.80 [95% CI, 3.58-4.04]), including the inpatient maternal mortality rate during the hospital delivery admission (273.0 vs 7.0 per 100 000 hospital deliveries; adjusted IRR, 14.24 [95% CI, 10.87-18.66]).

Conclusions and relevance: In this US cross-sectional study, the prevalence of hospital deliveries for past cancer survivors increased from 2016 to 2023, and severe maternal morbidity was increased at delivery for past and current cancer survivors. These findings support the importance of preconception evaluation for cancer survivors and early referral to tertiary care centers with multidisciplinary teams, as currently recommended by multiple organizations.

item.title: Neighborhood Exposure to Firearm Violence and Measures of Psychosocial Distress
item.description:
Importance: Exposure to firearm violence is believed to have substantial indirect health effects among those who experience and witness it.

Objective: To assess whether neighborhood firearm violence is associated with psychological and behavioral outcomes.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study links geocoded, individual-level data from adults participating in the 2021 and 2022 California Health Interview Surveys, a state-representative survey conducted annually by the UCLA Center for Health Policy Research linked to shooting events near interviewees' home from the Gun Violence Archive. Data analysis was performed from August to October 2025.

Exposure: Any shooting event occurring within 500 m of interviewees' households within the past 12 months (January 1, 2020, and December 31, 2022). Sensitivity analyses included any fatal shooting, any shooting within the past 2 months, and more than 1 shooting event.

Main outcome and measures: Primary outcomes were self-reported worry about experiencing firearm violence, feeling unsafe in one's neighborhood, heavy substance use, and psychological distress. Survey-adjusted multivariable Poisson regression models assessed the association between the exposure and each outcome.

Results: Among the 45 916 adults interviewed (mean [SD] age, 48.2 [18.7] years; 26 077 [51.8%] female), 6289 (17.2%, weighted) had a shooting occur near their home; there were no missing data. Polysubstance use was positively associated with most exposures, with the highest incident rate ratios (IRRs) among those experiencing a recent shooting in their neighborhood within the past 2 months (IRR, 1.41; 95% CI, 1.18-1.68) and those experiencing more than 1 shooting (IRR, 1.33; 95% CI, 1.14-1.55). The highest magnitude associations for each exposure were observed with the outcome of feeling unsafe in one's neighborhood among those experiencing a recent shooting event (IRR, 1.73; 95% CI, 1.52-1.97) or more than 1 shooting (IRR, 2.36; 95% CI, 2.17-2.56). All exposures had a positive association with worry about experiencing firearm violence, with IRRs of 1.14 (95% CI, 1.04-1.24) for those experiencing any shooting to 1.28 (95% CI, 1.13-1.43) for those experiencing more than 1 shooting in the past 12 months.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of the association between firearm violence and self-reported psychosocial distress, exposure to neighborhood firearm violence was associated with a range of outcomes that may affect people's perceptions of their safety and could potentially contribute to negative coping behaviors, such as substance use.

item.title: Sudden Deaths From Aneurysmal Subarachnoid Hemorrhage and Proximity to Neurosurgical Tertiary Care
item.description:
Importance: A substantial proportion of deaths due to aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) occur without admission to neurosurgical units. Whether this proportion varies by geographic region is unclear.

Objective: To determine the proportion of SAH deaths without neurosurgical unit admission across hospital districts in 2 high-income countries.

Design, setting, and participants: This retrospective, population-based cohort study used 2 externally validated nationwide administrative data collections in all 41 hospital districts and 10 neurosurgical units in Finland and New Zealand from January 1, 2001, to December 31, 2017. Participants included all hospitalized and fatal nonhospitalized cases with SAH. Data were analyzed from July 1, 2024, to September 7, 2026.

Exposures: Hospital district of residence and its distance to the designated neurosurgical referral center, grouped into 4 zones.

Main outcomes and measures: The primary outcome was the death-based proportion of all 30-day deaths after SAH that occurred without neurosurgical unit admission (prehospital deaths plus deaths within 30 days after admission to a nonneurosurgical unit divided by all 30-day deaths from SAH). This proportion was estimated across 41 hospital districts and demographic groups, with age- and sex-adjusted risk ratios (RRs) and 95% CIs.

Results: A total of 12 912 patients with SAH (7856 in Finland and 5056 in New Zealand; median age, 58 [IQR, 49-69] years; 7924 [61.4%] women) were included. Of all 5418 SAH deaths, 3819 (70.5%) occurred without neurosurgical unit admission: 2203 of 3114 (70.7%) in Finland (interdistrict range, 403 of 644 [62.6%] to 5 of 5 [100%]) and 1616 of 2304 (70.1%) in New Zealand (interdistrict range, 111 of 190 [58.4%] to 22 of 23 [95.7%]). Compared with districts containing a neurosurgical unit (1723 of 2602 [66.2%]), the death-based proportions were higher in close-distance (1-130 km; 796 of 1129 [70.5%]; RR, 1.07 [95% CI, 1.02-1.12]), middle-distance (131-157 km; 469 of 599 [78.3%]; RR, 1.18 [95% CI, 1.12-1.24]), and far-distance (158-371 km; 831 of 1088 [76.4%]; RR, 1.15 [95% CI, 1.10-1.20]) zones. This proportion increased by 6.7% (95% CI, 4.9%-8.5%) for each additional 100 km to a neurosurgical unit. The proportions decreased in both countries over time.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cohort study of 12 912 patients with SAH, most deaths occurred without neurosurgical unit admission, and this proportion increased with distance to the neurosurgical referral center. Prevention and early management outside tertiary care may therefore warrant priority in reducing SAH mortality.

item.title: Resistance Exercise Training for Depressive Symptoms: A Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression Analysis
item.description:
Importance: Resistance exercise training (RET) has established antidepressant effects compared with inactive control conditions; however, its effects vs active comparisons remain unclear.

Objective: To quantify the association of RET efficacy with active and inactive comparisons for depressive symptoms and explore variability across moderators.

Data sources: Published articles were identified using Google Scholar, MEDLINE, PubMed, Web of Science, and PsycInfo from inception to July 7, 2025.

Study selection: Randomized clinical trials (RCTs) with at least 3 weeks of RET or any non-RET comparison and a validated depressive symptom measure at baseline and at least 3 weeks were included. Active comparisons were aerobic exercise training, relaxation, flexibility, mind-body exercise, nutrition, education, advice or attention, mixed activities, and balance exercises. Inactive comparisons were no treatment, waiting lists, and continued usual care.

Data extraction and synthesis: Three reviewers independently extracted data. Meta-regression was used to test moderators, including primary moderators (age, sex, mental health status, RET duration, intensity, concealed allocation). Study quality was assessed using a modified Detsky scale.

Main outcomes and measures: All available associations of RET vs comparison conditions with depressive symptoms were quantified from baseline to at least 3 weeks. Random-effects models were used.

Results: Across 80 RCTs including 6123 participants (2880 participants [47.0%] in RET groups and 3243 [53.0%] in non-RET comparison groups; mean [SD] age, 57 [16] years; 3412 female [67.1%]), the number of effect sizes examined was 176; 57 RCTs enrolled participants with an illness. Resistance exercise training was associated with a significant, heterogenous, small-magnitude antidepressant effect size (Δ = 0.32 [95% CI, 0.25-0.39]; z = 9.31; P < .001) across all comparisons. The effect size was larger vs inactive comparisons (Δ = 0.54 [95% CI, 0.39-0.68]; z = 7.22; P < .001) than active comparisons (Δ = 0.21 [95% CI, 0.14-0.27]; z = 6.20; P < .001). Versus active comparisons, RET was associated with a significant, heterogenous, small-magnitude antidepressant effect size, with larger effect sizes among participants with a mental illness (Δ = 0.40 [95% CI, 0.29-0.50]) vs without a mental illness (Δ = 0.11 [95% CI, 0.04-0.18]). Versus inactive comparisons, RET was associated with a significant, heterogenous, moderate-magnitude antidepressant effect size, with larger effect sizes for all-female cohorts (Δ = 0.87 [95% CI, 0.60-1.14]), RET frequencies of at least 4 days per week (Δ = 0.46 [95% CI, 0.31-0.60]), and session durations of 30 minutes or less (Δ = 1.75 [95% CI, 0.97-2.54]), and smaller effect sizes with concealed allocation (Δ = 0.32 [95% CI, 0.20-0.44]).

Conclusions and relevance: This meta-analysis and meta-regression analysis found that RET was associated with moderate-magnitude, clinically meaningful reductions in depressive symptoms that were greater than other activities with antidepressant benefits, supporting the recommendation of RET in the treatment of depression.

item.title: Climate Vulnerability, Historical Redlining, and Children's Mental Health Care Use
item.description:
Importance: Structural inequities stemming from historical redlining and environmental injustice have created varying levels of risk among marginalized communities. However, the association of climate risk and structural racism with pediatric mental health care use remains underexplored.

Objectives: To examine associations between climate vulnerability and pediatric mental health care use, and to assess whether these associations vary by historical redlining status.

Design, setting, and participants: This cross-sectional study of children aged younger than 18 years residing in New York State between 2017 and 2022 used all-payer hospital administrative data from the New York State Department of Health. Statistical analysis was conducted from January 2025 through February 2026.

Main outcome and measures: Outcomes included mental health-related emergency department (ED) and outpatient visits identified using International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, Tenth Revision-coded mental health diagnosis subtypes (eg, depression, attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder), aggregated at the census-tract level. The primary exposure was climate-specific Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles (where 1 indicates low climate vulnerability and 4 indicates high climate vulnerability). Poisson regression models were conducted to examine associations between Climate Vulnerability Index quartiles and mental health-related health care utilization, including interactions with neighborhood-level redlining status (Home Owners' Loan Corporation grades C/D vs A/B) and subtype-specific analyses. Models adjusted for age, sex, self- or guardian-reported race and ethnicity, and neighborhood-level covariates, with coefficients reported as rate ratios (RRs).

Results: A total of 553 134 mental health-related visits were included (mean [SD] age, 7.2 [5.8] years; 285 526 male [51.6%]). Compared with children living in areas with the lowest climate vulnerability, those living in the highest-vulnerability areas had higher outpatient visit rates (RR, 1.98; 95% CI, 1.72-2.27) and non-statistically significantly higher ED visit rates (RR, 1.14; 95% CI, 0.96-1.35). Associations between high climate vulnerability and mental health-related health care utilization varied by redlining status. In historically redlined neighborhoods, high climate vulnerability was associated with outpatient health care utilization (RR, 1.47; 95% CI, 1.44-1.51; P < .001 for interaction) and, to a lesser extent, ED utilization (RR, 1.06; 95% CI, 1.02-1.09; P < .001 for interaction); in nonredlined neighborhoods high climate vulnerability was associated with lower outpatient health care utilization (RR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.45-0.49; P < .001 for interaction) and not associated with ED utilization (RR, 1.00; 95% CI, 0.93-1.07). Associations also varied across mental health diagnosis subtypes, with higher climate vulnerability associated with increased health care utilization for most diagnosis subtypes.

Conclusions and relevance: In this cross-sectional study of children, residence in historically redlined and climate-vulnerable neighborhoods was associated with higher rates of mental health-related health care utilization. These findings highlight geographic patterns in mental health-related health care utilization that may be relevant to future research on climate preparedness, mental health services, culturally responsive care, and access to services for children experiencing climate-related stressors and structural inequities.
